# What I would change

## The backend, honestly

- Turing.jl gave us submodels, a choice of samplers, and the rest of
  Julia. The proof of concept exists because of it, and choosing it was
  right at the time
- It is still 0.x. First release in 2017, current release v0.46.0 in
  July 2026
- Nine breaking releases from v0.37.0 to v0.46.0 in sixteen months. The
  paper's artefact is pinned to Turing 0.35. Porting `@submodel` to
  `to_submodel` is what it took to reach v0.46, which the maintained
  package now runs on
- Over the last six months one person has written most of the human
  commits to both Turing.jl and DynamicPPL.jl, where most of the
  composition machinery lives. Nobody else is in double figures

::: {.callout-important}
This is not a criticism of the people doing the work, which is good
work. It is a statement about how much of the stack rests on very few
of them.
:::

::: {.attribution}
Release dates and commit counts from the GitHub API on 2026-08-10,
`main` branches, human authors only
:::

## Automatic differentiation is the part that decided it

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
- Turing is tested most extensively against ForwardDiff, Enzyme,
  Mooncake, and ReverseDiff. Everything else routes through
  `DifferentiationInterface.jl`
- The one public table of which backends worked with which models,
  `ADTests`, was archived this month, so we run our own matrix
- For a model somebody acts on during an outbreak, a silently wrong
  gradient is not a footnote
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.callout-important}
## From the Turing.jl documentation
"not all AD libraries in there are thoroughly tested on Turing models.
Thus, it is possible that some of them will either error ... or maybe
even silently give incorrect results"
:::

## What it does not do yet

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- The component library stops at basic epidemiological patterns. No
  partial pooling, and no automatic mapping between latent and
  observed states
- Changing a component's order does not update the priors that go with
  it. That stays manual, and it is the part that would make
  specification quick
- Large simulated counts error, vectors mixing missing and observed
  values need handling by hand, and profiling through the layers is
  hard
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Other ways to do this**

- AlgebraicJulia gives formal compositional guarantees and little
  support for probabilistic models
- `JuliaBUGS.jl` and `RxInfer.jl` specify models as graphs, and
  `ModelingToolkit.jl` composes acausal components symbolically. Each
  trades some flexibility for structure

::: {.callout-note}
The component structure is also what makes this tractable for a
language model to assemble. That is a reason to keep the parts small.
:::
:::
::::
